questions.question: What are Docker and the cloud, and why should a fresher learn them early?
questions.title: Docker & Cloud Fundamentals
questions.direct_answer: Docker packages an application's user-space filesystem and runtime configuration as an image and runs isolated containers from it. Cloud computing provides on-demand infrastructure and managed services through provider APIs. A fresher benefits from knowing both because many backend teams use containers and cloud services—but neither is universal, and they do not eliminate environment, security, or operations work.

sections.title: Docker and Cloud Fundamentals
sections.content:
Docker and cloud computing solve different parts of delivery. Docker builds an image from application/user-space files and runtime configuration, then creates isolated containers from it. Cloud providers expose compute, storage, networking, and managed services through APIs.

A team can build one tested Java image and run that digest on a laptop, CI worker, or cloud container platform, while injecting environment-specific configuration. This improves repeatability but does not make CPU architecture, kernel behavior, network, data, and external services identical.

A fresher should learn the image/container lifecycle, ports, logs, volumes, health, and basic cloud responsibility/cost models. Many teams use these skills, while others deploy JARs, functions, or platform builds. The concepts are useful; the specific tooling follows the job.

sections.title: Core Concepts
sections.content: The core ideas: (1) a container image is an immutable, layered package — app + its runtime — that runs anywhere a compatible runtime exists, ending environment drift; (2) a container is isolated (namespaces/cgroups) but shares the host kernel, so it's lighter than a VM; (3) a Dockerfile is the recipe that builds the image; (4) the cloud is on-demand, billed-by-use infrastructure — compute (VMs, containers, serverless), storage, databases, networking — replacing hardware provisioning with API calls; (5) the shared-responsibility model — the cloud provider secures the platform, you secure what you put on it; (6) the deploy contract — a container image + cloud compute = a running service, reproducibly.

sections.title: Container vs. Bare App vs. Cloud VM
A minimal Dockerfile and the deploy-to-cloud idea
sections.content:
# A Dockerfile: the recipe that packages a Spring Boot jar into an image.
FROM eclipse-temurin:17-jre-alpine       # base: a JVM runtime
WORKDIR /app
COPY target/app.jar app.jar              # the app, copied in
EXPOSE 8080
ENTRYPOINT ["java","-jar","/app/app.jar"]

# Build the image once:  docker build -t myapp:1.0 .
# Run it anywhere:       docker run -p 8080:8080 myapp:1.0
#   The SAME image runs on a laptop, a CI runner, and a cloud VM/container
#   service -> environment drift is gone.

# Cloud deploy (idea): push the image to a registry, then ask the cloud to run it.
#   docker push registry.example.com/myapp:1.0
#   # on the cloud: "run this image, 3 replicas, behind a load balancer"
#   # The cloud provisions compute + networking on demand; you pay per use.
#   # The cloud provider secures the platform; you secure the app & secrets.

sections.title: Trade-offs & When It Matters
sections.content: The central tension for a fresher is 'this feels advanced' versus 'this is the default': containers and cloud can feel like senior topics, but they are the deployment model used from day one, so the right move is to learn the fundamentals (image, Dockerfile, on-demand compute) early, not defer them. A second tension: a container is lighter than a VM but shares the host kernel, so it's a weaker security boundary — relevant later, but worth knowing. The third: the cloud's pay-per-use model is cheap for experimentation but can surprise you on a forgotten running resource; learning to tag and clean up resources is a practical habit.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Docker packages an app + its runtime into a portable container image; the cloud provides on-demand, billed-by-use infrastructure — together they're the modern deploy model.
A container ends environment drift: the same image runs on a laptop, CI, and production.
A container shares the host kernel (lighter than a VM) but is a weaker security boundary — relevant as you grow.
A Dockerfile is the recipe that builds the image; build once, run anywhere with a compatible runtime.
The cloud replaces hardware provisioning with API calls, billed by use; the shared-responsibility model splits security between provider and you.
sections.content:
- Docker image: packaged filesystem layers plus runtime configuration.
- Container: an isolated runtime instance that shares its hosting kernel.
- Cloud: provider-operated compute, storage, networking, and higher-level services consumed on demand.
- Containers improve environment consistency but do not make hardware, kernel, data, and external dependencies identical.
- Learn the concepts early, then follow the actual deployment model used by the team.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Docker packages application files, user-space dependencies, and runtime configuration into an image and creates isolated containers from it. Cloud computing provides provider-operated infrastructure and managed services on demand. They often meet when CI builds a Java image, a registry stores its digest, and a cloud container service runs it with production configuration.

For example, I can build and test an order-service image locally, push it, and deploy that exact digest to a managed container platform connected to a database and queue. The image reduces differences in the application runtime, while the cloud supplies capacity and services.

Neither tool removes engineering work. Containers share a hosting kernel and still depend on data, network, secrets, and platform architecture. Cloud scaling and availability must be configured and tested, and cost follows many meters. Learning them early is valuable because they are common delivery concepts—not because every backend role uses Docker or every application belongs in a cloud.

An image packages application files, user-space dependencies, and runtime configuration; the container still uses the hosting kernel and external services. sections.title: Docker: Packaging Applications with Their Environment
sections.content:
Docker is a **containerization platform** that bundles your application code, runtime libraries, and system dependencies into a single, portable unit called a **container**.

Think of it like a shipping container for software: just as physical shipping containers move goods reliably across trucks, ships, and trains, Docker containers move applications reliably across developer laptops, test servers, and production clouds.

The core problem Docker solves is **environment inconsistency**—the infamous "it works on my machine" issue. Before Docker, a Spring Boot app might work perfectly on your laptop (macOS with Java 17) but fail in production (Linux with Java 11 and different library versions). Docker eliminates this by packaging the exact Java runtime, OS libraries, and configuration your app needs, guaranteeing identical behavior everywhere.

sections.title: Key Ideas at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Problem: Works on My Machine|~Environment drift breaks deploys|dev JDK 17 vs prod JDK 11|missing libs and config|app fails in production
blue|Docker Image|~Read-only app package|JAR + JRE + OS libs|built from a Dockerfile|same bytes everywhere
emerald|Docker Container|~Running instance of an image|isolated process|starts in milliseconds|shares host kernel
violet|Why It Wins|~One artifact, all stages|laptop = CI = prod|Docker Hub shares images|standard Java deploy unit

sections.title: Dockerizing a Spring Boot Application
When to Use Docker
sections.content:
Use Docker when you need **consistent environments across teams**—if five developers are working on a Spring Boot microservice, Docker ensures everyone runs the exact same Java version, library dependencies, and OS configuration.

Use it for **simplified local development**—instead of manually installing PostgreSQL, Redis, and Kafka on your laptop, run them as Docker containers with a single command.

Use it for **cloud deployment**—every major cloud platform (AWS ECS, Google Cloud Run, Azure Container Instances) runs Docker containers natively, making your app instantly portable across providers. Docker is now the default packaging format for Java backend services in production.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Confusing containers with VMs**: Freshers often think Docker is a lightweight virtual machine. Containers share the host OS kernel and start in milliseconds, while VMs virtualize hardware and take minutes to boot.
- **Copying the entire project folder**: Beginners write `COPY . /app` in Dockerfiles, including source code, .git folders, and IDE files. Only copy the compiled JAR—Docker images should contain the production artifact, not development clutter.
- **Running as root user**: Default Docker containers run as root, which is a security risk. Production Dockerfiles should create a non-root user and switch to it before running the application.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- Docker builds immutable images and creates containers from them.
- Images package application/user-space files and configuration, not a separate kernel.
- Containers use kernel isolation and resource controls supplied by the host/runtime.
- A pinned image improves repeatability across stages.
- Runtime configuration, architecture, data, external services, and security still affect behavior.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Docker is a platform and toolchain for building images and creating isolated containers. An image contains application files, user-space dependencies, and runtime configuration. When a container is created, the runtime adds isolation, networking, mounts, resource controls, and a writable layer while sharing the hosting kernel.

For example, CI can build one Spring Boot image from a pinned JRE base, run tests/scans, and promote the same image digest through staging and production. Each environment supplies its own database address and secrets rather than changing the JAR inside the container.

This reduces the 'works on my machine' problem, but it does not make every machine identical. CPU architecture, kernel, runtime configuration, volumes, networks, and external services can still differ. Docker solves repeatable packaging and container lifecycle; orchestration, persistent data, security policy, monitoring, and application correctness remain separate responsibilities.

questions.question: How do a Docker image and a container work together?
questions.direct_answer: A Docker image is the packaged, read-only content and configuration used to create containers. Docker creates a container from that image, then adds runtime settings and a writable layer. One image can create many separate containers, and stopping a container is different from removing it.
follow_up_questions: What happens to data written to a container when the container stops?

sections.title: Images and Containers: The Blueprint and the Running Instance
sections.content:
A **Docker image** is the packaged application content and configuration used as the starting point for containers. It contains filesystem layers and settings such as the default command. A digest identifies image content, while a tag such as `orders:1.4` is a movable name that can point to a digest.

When Docker **creates a container**, it combines those read-only image layers with runtime configuration, isolation, networking, mounts, resource controls, and a container-specific writable layer. Starting the container launches its configured process. Stopping it ends that process but normally keeps the container and writable layer; removing the container discards that layer unless the data was stored separately.

The class-and-object comparison is a useful first picture because one image can create many containers. It is not exact: a container is an operating-system runtime resource, and an image tag is not a fixed Java type identity.

sections.title: Key Ideas at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Build|~Create image content|Dockerfile + context|filesystem layers|config + digest
blue|Create|~Make a container|choose image|add runtime settings|add writable layer
emerald|Start and use|~Run its process|network + ports|mounts + limits|logs and health
violet|Stop or remove|~Different lifecycle actions|stop keeps container|start it again|remove discards writable layer

sections.title: Build One Image, Run Many Containers
sections.content:
```bash
# Build one image and see its content identifier.
docker build -t orders:1.4 .
docker image inspect orders:1.4 --format '{{.Id}}'

# Create two separate containers from that image.
docker run -d --name orders-a -p 8081:8080 orders:1.4
docker run -d --name orders-b -p 8082:8080 orders:1.4

# Stopping does not remove the first container.
docker stop orders-a
docker start orders-a

# Removing a container does not remove the image.
docker rm -f orders-b
docker image ls orders
```

rows: Runtime instance created from an image
Its writable layer and runtime state can change
Volume, bind mount, or external data service

sections.title: When to Use Each Concept
sections.content:
Build or select an **image** when choosing the exact application artifact to distribute. Create and run a **container** when that artifact needs a runtime instance with a specific port, network, configuration, secret, mount, or resource limit.

For example, CI can build `orders:1.4`, record its digest, and push it to a registry. Development, staging, and production can create containers from that digest while supplying different database addresses and secrets. The application content is the same, but platform architecture, runtime configuration, data, and external services can still differ.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Editing a container as if it updates the image**: a manual file change belongs only to that container's writable layer. Change the build input and create a new image instead.
- **Treating stop and remove as the same action**: a stopped container can normally be started again; a removed container must be created again.
- **Using a tag as proof of content**: a tag can move. Use or record the image digest when exact identity matters.
- **Keeping important data only in the writable layer**: place durable data in a volume, bind mount, or external service.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- An image supplies packaged application content and configuration.
- A container is created from an image with runtime settings and a writable layer.
- One image can create many independent containers.
- Stop keeps a container; remove deletes that container and its writable layer.
- Tags can move, while a digest identifies image content.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A Docker image and a container are two stages of the same lifecycle. The image is the packaged application content and configuration. Docker uses it as the read-only base when it creates a container, then adds runtime configuration, isolation, networking, mounts, resource controls, and a writable layer.

For example, CI may build one `orders:1.4` image. I can create `orders-a` on host port 8081 and `orders-b` on 8082 from that same image. They share the image content but have different container IDs, runtime settings, processes, and writable layers.

A container can be created, running, paused, or stopped; it is not only a running process. Stopping it normally keeps the writable layer so it can start again. Removing it discards that container layer, while the image remains available. For durable data I use a volume or external store, and for exact release identity I record a digest because a tag can move.

questions.question: How does a typical Docker workflow look for a Spring Boot application?
questions.direct_answer: Build your Spring Boot JAR with ./mvnw test && ./mvnw package, write a Dockerfile specifying the base JDK image and startup command, build the Docker image with docker build, test locally with docker run, then push to a registry like Docker Hub with docker push for deployment to staging or production.
follow_up_questions: What does the -p flag do in docker run?
What is Docker Hub vs Amazon ECR vs Google Container Registry?

sections.title: End-to-End Docker Workflow for Spring Boot
sections.content:
The Docker workflow for Spring Boot follows a clear sequence: **build your application artifact**, **define the runtime environment**, **create the image**, **test it locally**, and **distribute it for deployment**. First, you compile your Spring Boot project into an executable JAR using Maven or Gradle.

Then you write a **Dockerfile** that specifies a base Java image, copies your JAR, exposes the port your app listens on, and defines the startup command. Next, you build the Docker image using `docker build`, which creates a versioned, immutable package containing your app and its runtime. You test the image locally by running it as a container with `docker run`, verifying endpoints and behavior. Finally, you push the image to a **container registry** like Docker Hub, AWS ECR, or Google Container Registry, where CI/CD pipelines or production servers can pull it for deployment. This workflow is the industry standard for deploying Java microservices today.

sections.title: Key Ideas at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|1. Build JAR|~Compile with Maven|./mvnw test && ./mvnw package|produces target/app.jar|the deployable artifact
blue|2. Build Image|~Wrap JAR in an image|docker build -t app:1.0 .|reads the Dockerfile|tagged and versioned
emerald|3. Run and Test|~Verify locally|docker run -p 8080:8080|map host to container port|curl the endpoints
violet|4. Push and Deploy|~Ship to a registry|docker push to Hub or ECR|CI/CD automates it|K8s or ECS pulls it

sections.title: Complete Spring Boot Docker Workflow
When to Use This Workflow
sections.content:
Use this workflow **every time you prepare a Spring Boot app for deployment beyond your local machine**—whether it's for a staging environment, production, or sharing with your team. It's essential when working in **microservices architectures**, where each service is independently packaged and deployed as a container.

Use it when setting up **CI/CD pipelines**—your Jenkins or GitHub Actions job would run these exact steps automatically on every commit to the main branch.

Use it when **deploying to cloud platforms**—AWS ECS, Google Cloud Run, Azure Container Instances, and Kubernetes all expect Docker images as the deployment unit. Modern Java backend development treats this workflow as a baseline skill, not an advanced DevOps topic.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Building the Docker image before the JAR**: Freshers write the Dockerfile and run `docker build` before running `mvn package`, so the COPY instruction fails because the JAR doesn't exist yet. Always compile first.
- **Including unnecessary files in the image**: Using `COPY . /app` copies your entire project—source code, .git folder, IDE configs—into the image. Only copy the JAR. Use a .dockerignore file to exclude everything except the target directory.
- **Forgetting to expose the port**: If your Dockerfile doesn't have `EXPOSE 8080` and you don't map ports with `-p` when running, you can't reach the application from outside the container. The app runs but is inaccessible.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: **./mvnw test && ./mvnw package**: compiles your Spring Boot app into an executable JAR in the target directory, which is the artifact you'll copy into the Docker image
**Dockerfile**: a text file with instructions to build an image—FROM specifies the base image, COPY adds files, EXPOSE documents the port, ENTRYPOINT defines the startup command
**docker build**: reads the Dockerfile and creates an immutable image by executing each instruction as a layer, tagging the result with a name and version
**docker run**: creates and starts a container from an image, with flags like -p for port mapping, -e for environment variables, and -d for detached mode
**docker push**: uploads an image to a container registry so other machines can pull and run it, enabling distribution across environments

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A typical Spring Boot container workflow starts by testing and packaging the application, then building an immutable image from a reviewed Dockerfile. CI should tag the image meaningfully, scan it, and push it to a registry. Deployment references the image digest or controlled tag and supplies environment-specific configuration, secrets, networking, storage, and health policy.

For example, a multi-stage Dockerfile can run `./mvnw test package` in a JDK stage and copy the JAR into a runtime stage. Locally I run it with a published port and a development configuration. CI pushes the tested image, and the target platform replaces containers gradually while checking readiness.

I do not rebuild a different binary for each environment or patch running containers. I also do not assume the same image guarantees the same outcome: database versions, CPU architecture, mounted config, limits, and external services still matter. The image is the repeatable artifact within a larger release process.

questions.question: What is Docker Compose and when would you use it?
questions.direct_answer: Docker Compose is a tool for defining and running multi-container applications using a YAML file. Use it when your Spring Boot app depends on other services—like PostgreSQL for data, Redis for caching, or Kafka for messaging—so you can start the entire stack with one docker compose up command.
follow_up_questions: What is the difference between Docker Compose and Kubernetes?
How do you persist data across Docker Compose restarts?

sections.title: Quick revision
content: **docker-compose.yml**: a YAML file defining services (containers), networks, and volumes for a multi-container application in declarative format
**docker compose up**: starts all services defined in the YAML file, creating containers, networks, and volumes as needed in a single command
**Service networking**: Compose creates a default network where each service is reachable by its service name as a hostname, enabling container-to-container communication
**depends_on**: specifies startup order so a Spring Boot app waits for the database container to start before launching, though it doesn't wait for the database to be ready
**Volumes**: persist data across container restarts by mapping container paths to named volumes or host directories, essential for databases

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Docker Compose describes a multi-container application in a YAML file. Each service can define an image or build, environment, commands, ports, networks, volumes, dependencies, and health checks. `docker compose up` creates the declared resources and starts or recreates the services.

For example, a Spring Boot `api` service and PostgreSQL `db` service join the default Compose network. The API uses `db` as the database host, while a named volume holds the database files when the container is replaced. `depends_on` can express ordering and, with supported health conditions, wait for health—but the application should still retry a temporarily unavailable database.

Compose is excellent for local development, demos, integration tests, and some single-host deployments. It is not a multi-node cluster orchestrator, and a Compose file should not contain committed production passwords. I use it to make a small application topology reproducible, not as proof that every dependency is ready or highly available.

sections.title: Build the mental model
sections.content:
Docker Compose defines a multi-container application in YAML: services, images/builds, networks, volumes, environment, dependencies, and health checks. `docker compose up` creates the declared resources and starts or recreates services so a team can run the same local topology repeatedly.

For example, a Spring Boot API can use the service name `db` to reach a PostgreSQL service on the Compose network. A named volume can preserve database data when the container is recreated. `depends_on` controls startup ordering and can use health conditions in supported Compose behavior, but it does not replace application retries or readiness handling.

Compose is useful for development, integration tests, demos, and some single-host deployments. It is not a multi-node orchestrator and should not contain committed production secrets. Use environment files carefully or a secret mechanism appropriate to the target platform.

sections.title: Key Ideas at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|The Problem|~Multi-container setup|app plus DB plus cache|manual docker run is messy|painful onboarding
blue|docker-compose.yml|~Declare the stack|services, ports, env|one YAML file|version controlled
emerald|One Command|~docker compose up|starts all services|auto networking by name|down tears it all
violet|Scope|~Local dev and testing|not production|K8s or ECS for prod|fast team onboarding

sections.title: When to Use Docker Compose
sections.content:
Use Compose when your Spring Boot application **depends on external services during development**—if you need PostgreSQL to store orders, Redis to cache user sessions, and RabbitMQ for async messaging, Compose lets you start all three with one command instead of juggling multiple terminals.

Use it for **onboarding new team members**—instead of a ten-page wiki on installing Postgres, Kafka, and configuring connection strings, they clone the repo and run `docker compose up`.

Use it for **integration testing** where your tests need a real database—you can start the stack, run tests, and tear it down in your CI pipeline.

Use it when **prototyping microservices locally**—spin up three Spring Boot apps with their own databases to simulate a distributed system. Don't use Compose for production orchestration—that's Kubernetes territory. Compose is for development simplicity.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using Compose in production**: Freshers sometimes think Compose is a production orchestration tool like Kubernetes. It's not—Compose lacks high availability, scaling when configured, rolling updates, and health checks needed in production. Use Kubernetes or managed services for production.
- **Hardcoding sensitive data in docker-compose.yml**: Putting real database passwords directly in the YAML file that gets committed to Git is a security risk. Use environment files like .env and add them to .gitignore, then reference with ${DB_PASSWORD} syntax.
- **Not understanding service names as hostnames**: Compose automatically creates a network where services reach each other by their service name. If your service is named `db`, your Spring Boot app connects to `jdbc:postgresql://db:5432`, not `localhost:5432`.

sections.title: A minimal Dockerfile and the deploy-to-cloud idea
sections.content:
```text
# A Dockerfile: the recipe that packages a Spring Boot jar into an image.
FROM eclipse-temurin:17-jre-alpine       # base: a JVM runtime
WORKDIR /app
COPY target/app.jar app.jar              # the app, copied in
EXPOSE 8080
ENTRYPOINT ["java","-jar","/app/app.jar"]

# Build the image once:  docker build -t myapp:1.0 .
# Run it anywhere:       docker run -p 8080:8080 myapp:1.0
#   The SAME image runs on a laptop, a CI runner, and a cloud VM/container
#   service -> environment drift is gone.

# Cloud deploy (idea): push the image to a registry, then ask the cloud to run it.
#   docker push registry.example.com/myapp:1.0
#   # on the cloud: "run this image, 3 replicas, behind a load balancer"
#   # The cloud provisions compute + networking on demand; you pay per use.
#   # The cloud provider secures the platform; you secure the app & secrets.
```

sections.title: Important trade-off
sections.content: A Docker image is a read-only template containing your application code, dependencies, and runtime—like a blueprint. A Docker container is a running instance of that image—like an object created from a class. You can launch multiple containers from the same image, each with its own state.

questions.question: What role does Docker play in modern Java backend deployment?
questions.title: Docker's Role in Modern Java Backend Deployment
questions.direct_answer: Docker can provide a repeatable image as the handoff between a Java build and a runtime platform. CI may build and scan the image, a registry stores it, and a container service or orchestrator runs that same digest with environment-specific configuration. Docker is common but not required: Java applications are also deployed as JARs, native executables, platform builds, or functions.

sections.title: Docker as the Deployment Standard for Java Backends
sections.content:
A container image is one common **release artifact** for a Java backend. A build pipeline can package the JAR and runtime files, identify the result by digest, scan/sign it, and store it in a registry. A runtime platform then creates containers from that image with environment-specific configuration and policy.

This separates build from run and makes rollback/promotion easier to reason about. It does not mean the image runs identically on every architecture or that orchestration automatically scales, heals the application, or provides zero downtime. Probes, replica policy, draining, compatibility, data migration, and rollback still need design.

Docker is not universal. Direct JARs, WARs, buildpacks, native executables, and functions remain valid. Its role is strongest where an OCI image is the agreed handoff between development and operations.

sections.title: Key Ideas at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Build|~Create the artifact|compile and test JAR|build image|scan/sign|identify digest
blue|Distribute|~Registry|push immutable content|control tags|promote digest|retain rollback images
emerald|Run|~Container platform|inject config/secrets|network + storage|probes and limits|replica policy
violet|Boundary|~Not automatic|data migration|application correctness|architecture compatibility|rollout/rollback design

sections.title: Spring Boot Production Dockerfile with Best Practices
When Docker Becomes Essential
sections.content:
Use Docker when the team wants an OCI image as a repeatable artifact, depends on container scheduling, or needs a consistent user-space runtime across build and deployment stages. Prefer another packaging model when the platform already provides a simpler buildpack/function/JAR workflow and an image adds no useful boundary.

The decision includes registry operations, patching/rebuilds, signing, vulnerability response, base-image ownership, architecture targets, and runtime observability—not only writing a Dockerfile.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Calling Docker universal**: learn the deployment model actually used by the system.
- **Using a moving tag as release identity**: deploy a controlled tag or digest.
- **Expecting orchestration to guarantee zero downtime**: design readiness, draining, capacity, data compatibility, and rollback.
- **Baking secrets or environment config into the image**: inject them through the runtime platform.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- An image can be the versioned deployment artifact produced by CI.
- Registries distribute images; digests identify exact content.
- Runtime platforms inject environment-specific configuration, secrets, networking, and storage.
- Scanning, signing, least privilege, health checks, and observability remain separate responsibilities.
- Docker is one common delivery path, not the definition of Java production deployment.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Docker can make a container image the release artifact between a Java build and its runtime platform. CI compiles/tests the JAR, builds and scans the image, and pushes it to a registry. Deployment references a digest and supplies runtime configuration, secrets, network, volumes, limits, and health behavior.

For example, one `orders@sha256:...` image can be promoted from staging to production without rebuilding its application content. A container service or Kubernetes may run several instances and replace them during a rollout, but scaling happens only when replicas or autoscaling policies are configured.

Docker is common, not mandatory. A Java service can also run directly as a JAR on a VM, use a PaaS buildpack, compile to a native executable, or run as a function. I choose Docker when image portability, dependency packaging, registry promotion, and container scheduling provide a clear operational benefit, while still handling signing, least privilege, observability, and persistent data separately.
